Elekta (EKTA.B-SE) · Investment memo

Elekta: a delivered margin recovery carries FY27 on its own, but at a fair multiple of about 14 times the shares offer earnings growth and dividends, not the doubling implied by the guideline multiple

17 November 2026. Share price SEK 62.40 (close, 13 November 2026). Next report: Q2 FY27 on 25 November 2026.

How to read the figures. "FY27" is Elekta's financial year to 30 April 2027 (the company's FY2026/27), and the other years follow the same pattern. EBIT and gross margin are the company's adjusted measures. EPS is on the brokers' adjusted basis, and its base year is an underlying FY26 EPS of SEK 3.45. The headline consensus EPS growth of 68 percent for FY27 is measured from a tax-distorted FY26 figure of SEK 2.43 and should be ignored. The source and status of the forecasts are in end-note 1.

#0 Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

The case in one paragraph. Elekta is the number two in a radiotherapy industry dominated by two players. In fourteen months a new chief executive from outside the company has repaired the things the company controls: cost, price, order quality and accounting. The repair turns an earnings line that grew about 3 percent a year for six years into one that rises 21 percent this year (EPS from SEK 3.45 to SEK 4.18) and about 9 percent a year afterwards (SEK 4.95 in FY29), on revenue growth of only about 4 percent a year, half of which is price. The margin half of the case is delivered. The revenue half is not delivered, and the base case does not pretend otherwise: it assumes that Elekta keeps ceding unit share to Varian and United Imaging.

SEK 330mcost saving already in the run-rate, against a forecast FY27 EBIT rise of about SEK 310m
3.45 → 4.18EPS in SEK, FY26 underlying to FY27: +21%, then about 9% a year
1 pt = 8%of EPS for one point of gross margin, against about 3% for one point of revenue growth
14x, not 24xfair multiple today (16x if the thesis broadens), against Viewforth's guideline multiple of 24.09x

The six conclusions that matter.

  1. FY27 needs nothing new to happen. The whole forecast rise in FY27 EBIT (about SEK 310m) is smaller than the incremental cost saving already in the run-rate (about SEK 330m), so every other moving part only has to net to zero. Such coverage is rare for a company with Elekta's record, and it is the least-recognised point in the sell-side's work.
  2. The skew towards estimate upgrades is positive, but narrow in size, place and time. The skew sits in one line (the FY27 margin) and one window (the next six months). The base case has an FY27 margin of 13.7 percent, against guidance of 12.5 to 13.5 percent and consensus of about 13.2 percent. A plausible downside error lands FY27 EPS on consensus; a plausible upside error lands it about 7 percent above consensus. The skew is therefore favourable, worth 1 to 3 percent of EPS in the central case, but it is not unusual.
  3. FY28 decides the case, and the FY28 risks are dated and correlated. In FY28 the tariff refunds drop out, the hedged dollar rate steps down, Varian's new Accela platform reaches the market, and China's bidding deadline may have pulled orders forward into FY27. The FY28 forecast needs one strength that Elekta has not yet shown: holding a gross margin near 40 percent while hardware volume returns.
  4. The gross margin, not revenue, is the swing variable. One point of gross margin moves EPS by about 8 percent; one point of revenue growth moves EPS by about 3 percent. The gross margin is also the line that erased Elekta's last two improvement attempts.
  5. The share price has already paid for the worry clearing. Since late September the two-year-forward multiple has risen from about 11.6 to 13.4 times with consensus EPS unchanged. From here the return has to come from earnings, dividends and, only if revenue confirms the thesis, a broadening of the thesis.
  6. The fair multiple is where this memo parts company with Viewforth's guideline. The guideline fair multiple is 24.09 times, and the model's return at that multiple is +107 percent to January 2028, of which 80 points come from the multiple. I think about 14 times is fair in the current phase and about 16 times is fair if the thesis broadens. On that view the return is about +17 to +22 percent to January 2028 and about 14 to 15 percent a year to mid-2029, almost all of it from earnings growth and a 4 percent dividend yield. That return is the one this work supports.

The five judgements that move the value of the shares most over one to two years (the step-by-step arithmetic is in #9).

Three observable signals, arriving in a set order, would turn a favourable skew into an unusually favourable one. With all three signals, FY28 EPS would move towards SEK 4.90 to 5.00 (about 10 percent above the base case) and the multiple would have a reasoned path to 16 times. Without them, the shares offer a sound earnings-and-dividend return at a fair price.

#1 Tailwinds and headwinds in the operating environment

The operating environment has improved from adverse to a mild net headwind: it offers Elekta volume, withholds share and price, and its sharpest risks fall in FY28 rather than now.

The radiotherapy market itself is healthy. The market is worth about USD 7bn to 7.5bn and grows 5 to 8 percent a year, supported by an ageing US installed base (the average linear accelerator, or linac, is about 14 years old) and low penetration in emerging markets. Two things have changed in the last six months.

  • China is unfreezing. A two-year anti-corruption freeze cut the Chinese radiotherapy market by 40 to 50 percent. Hospital equipment procurement then rose 60 percent year on year in September 2026, and every province must run at least one round of bidding for standard linacs by the end of 2026. Elekta's Chinese orders have risen for three quarters while its Chinese sales fell 16 percent in Q1, so the Chinese recovery is in Elekta's order book but not yet in its revenue. Elekta's Beijing plant is about 90 percent localised, qualifies for the local-maker preference and has won more than half of centralised bids.
  • Competition has renewed itself on both flanks. Varian (part of Siemens Healthineers) launched its Accela platform in late September 2026, and Siemens signed more than EUR 400m of bundled hospital partnerships in one quarter. In China, United Imaging has grown from under 10 percent to over 30 percent of radiotherapy in five years and now leads new sales.

Regulation is mildly helpful, with one open tail risk. The helpful items are US tariff refunds, US clearance for Elekta's Evo linac in January 2026 and the shelving of a US bundled-payment model. The open tail risk is a Section 232 duty on the linacs that Elekta builds in Crawley, in the UK, for the US market.

The tailwinds are market-level volume, while the headwinds bear specifically on Elekta's share and price. Market volume is captured disproportionately by the leader (Varian) and the local champion in China (United Imaging). The environment therefore sets a ceiling on Elekta's growth (market growth of 5 to 6 percent) and decides how much of the self-help reaches revenue; the investment case does not rest on the environment.

Tailwinds: market-level volume

  • Market about USD 7bn to 7.5bn, growing 5 to 8% a year
  • Ageing US installed base (average linac about 14 years)
  • China unfreezing: procurement +60% in September 2026; bidding deadline end-2026; Elekta's Beijing plant about 90% localised
  • Mild regulatory help: tariff refunds, Evo's US clearance, 7.7% US procedure rate rise

Captured disproportionately by the leader and the local champion.

Headwinds: Elekta's share and price

  • Varian's Accela (USD 4m to 5m) and Siemens' bundles: the test moves to FY28 and FY29
  • United Imaging from under 10% to over 30% of Chinese radiotherapy
  • Chinese centralised procurement widening to a surveyed 20 to 40% by 2028
  • Section 232 duty tail; hedged dollar rate stepping down for FY28

Specific to Elekta: they decide how much self-help reaches revenue.

The competitive test from Accela has arrived later and more slowly than feared. Neither Siemens nor Elekta reports an order pause after the Accela launch. Accela is priced at USD 4m to 5m, with US approval expected in early 2027 and meaningful sales in FY28. The competitive risk has therefore moved from "orders pause this winter" to "price and share in FY28 and FY29", including pressure from older Varian systems repriced beneath Accela.

China runs the other way: Chinese sales should turn up earlier, and Chinese price pressure should arrive later. Brokers expect Elekta's Chinese sales to rise from Q2 FY27. Price pressure follows as centralised procurement widens from under 10 percent of Chinese radiotherapy to a surveyed 20 to 40 percent by 2028.

Two feared tail risks have eased. China's restrictions on European bidders exempt foreign companies that manufacture locally, which covers Elekta's Beijing plant. The final 2027 US outpatient payment rule offsets its cut to hospital drug payments with a 7.7 percent rate rise for procedures.

Currency pulls in opposite directions: translation helps reported sales in FY27, while the lower hedged dollar rate hurts the FY28 gross margin. Two brokers report that exchange rates have turned from a drag to a help for reported sales in the second half of FY27, and the base case carries about 0.7 point of that help in FY27 revenue. The evidence for the 0.7 point is broker statements rather than exchange rates, and it is not uniform (Deutsche Bank still assumes a headwind), so the 0.7 point should be held loosely; it changes reported sales, not the case. At the same time Elekta's hedged dollar rate steps down from SEK 10.12 in Q1 FY27 to SEK 9.14 for FY28, and FY28 is thinly hedged, so the gross margin loses a cushion just as tariff refunds end. The exposure that matters is the US dollar (in which Elekta earns revenue) against sterling (in which it incurs cost), not the krona against all currencies.

Against the market. The market reads the situation as "China clearing, sector rotating" and has re-rated the whole cohort; I agree on Chinese volume. I differ in two places. First, the market over-weights the near-term Accela scare and under-weights the FY28 price channel. Second, the market's China story is a volume story in which price barely features.

Strongest counter-case. I may be too cautious: a replacement cycle, Elekta's first clean adaptive-therapy product in a decade and the best-positioned foreign plant in China could give Elekta market-rate volume. If so, the base case is too low by about two points of revenue growth a year (sized in #3).

What would change my view. Americas orders still growing in the Q2 and Q3 reports, together with Chinese sales turning positive, would move the environment to neutral or better. A Section 232 duty, or a provincial price war in standard-linac tenders, would move the environment to a clear headwind.

Score: 46, set by the Rater. The end market is healthy (USD 7-7.5bn growing 5-8%, an ageing US base, China's procurement up 60% with a 2026 bidding deadline, mild regulatory help), but the forces that bear on Elekta's own revenue and margin are its competitors' renewal (Varian's Accela and Siemens bundles, United Imaging now leading China), China's centralised pricing widening by 2028, a Section 232 tail and a hedged dollar rate stepping down for FY28, so the volume tailwind is taken disproportionately by the leader and the local champion. Consensus sales growth of 3.5% (31st percentile) fits a slightly negative net balance; in line with the External group's 44 and the Analyst's mild net headwind, it sits just below Kerry's neutral environment and above Carlsberg's mature one.

#2 Internally driven corporate change

The internal change forces are strong, broad and already banked in the margin and in the quality of earnings, enough to carry FY27 on their own; they are thin on growth and carry real people risk.

The change is broad, fast and visible in the accounts, not only on slides.

  • People. A chief executive from outside the company and the industry (in post since late summer 2025), a new chief financial officer (March 2026) and a new chief operating officer (August 2026); four of the six executive seats have been refilled.
  • Cost. More than 500 roles (about 10 percent of the workforce) and three management layers removed; run-rate savings above SEK 500m, fully in place from Q1 FY27.
  • Price. A pricing desk with floor prices and walk-away rules; double-digit increases on service contracts; Evo priced about 30 percent above the legacy linac at a similar cost.
  • Quality of earnings. SEK 2.2bn of stale orders cancelled without refunds; SEK 1.4bn of failed development written off; capitalised development cut from about 60 percent of R&D towards 40 percent; a cash EBIT margin now published beside adjusted EBIT, and in Q1 the cash margin exceeded the adjusted margin.
  • Structure and targets. Five regions with their own profit and loss accounts; mid-term targets set in June 2026 (see #4).

The reset is a change in standards, and standards persist longer than programmes. Q1 FY27 shows what the new standards produce: operating costs flat on a year earlier despite about 190 basis points of accounting drag, and adjusted EBIT up 68 percent on sales down 3 percent.

The cost saving alone covers the FY27 EBIT rise (conclusion 1 of the summary), and the way the saving phases through the year makes FY27 easier, not harder. The saving is largest against the first three quarters' comparisons and small against the fourth quarter's, where the base case already assumes a lower margin than a year earlier (17.5 against 18.9 percent). FY27 therefore does not need a heroic fourth quarter.

The change does not yet include a growth programme. The resources behind the revenue leg are one product cycle (Evo), a regional sales model and software partnerships. Elekta answers its software gap against Varian through partners, not through a visible plan to out-integrate Varian. Acquisitions, buybacks and new geographies are absent from the plan, and the current phase does not need them.

Three cautions about the internal change are easy to miss.

  • Elekta has run a cost programme before, and its gains washed out. The FY23 programme (SEK 450m) was delivered in full and left no lasting margin gain, because logistics inflation and price concessions consumed it. The new protections (the pricing desk, price floors, indexation clauses and a cleaner backlog) are real, but they are processes that have not yet been tested by a period of rising input costs, which brokers expect from the second half of FY27.
  • The organisation is strained. The employee net promoter score is 6 against a target of 30, the chief commercial officer role has been abolished, and there is no bench behind the chief executive and the chief financial officer. A slower installation ramp for Evo would be the first symptom of the strain.
  • One alignment signal is unverified. Earlier work on Elekta leaned on the chief executive's open-market purchase of one million shares (about SEK 48m), reported by DNB Carnegie in September 2025. The research for this memo could not find the purchase in insider filings, and the FY26 remuneration report shows his direct holding as nil; the shares may be held indirectly. Until the purchase is checked against the insider register, the case should not rest on it. The verified insider purchase is small: a director bought 10,000 shares at SEK 51.82 in June 2026.

Against the market. The sell-side universally agrees that the margin leg is delivered. I differ in degree: the cautious brokers still treat the cost programme as one input among many, when the cost programme alone covers the year's earnings step.

Strongest counter-case. A 10 percent headcount cut, in a company with years of pay rises below inflation, could hollow out service and commercial capability, so that the saving is paid back in lost orders and a wage catch-up. The base case carries operating costs growing 3.5 percent a year from FY28 to allow for that risk.

What would change my view. Operating costs drifting above about SEK 1.15bn a quarter; a further large "one-off" charge (such charges have recurred in two consecutive fourth quarters); or the departure of either of the two people on whom the reset depends.

Score: 70, set by the Rater. A broad reset already in the accounts: new CEO, CFO and COO with four of six executive seats refilled, 10% of roles and three layers cut for over SEK 500m of run-rate savings, a pricing desk, SEK 2.2bn of stale orders cancelled and capitalisation cut, giving adjusted EBIT +68% on sales -3% in Q1 and alone covering the FY27 EBIT step; it is a change in standards, not only a cost programme. It is held below the Internal group's 74 because it is repair without a growth leg, the FY23 programme washed out, the organisation is strained (eNPS 6, empty bench) and the CEO's large purchase is unverified, so it sits just below Theon's deliberate pivot and above OEM's change of control.

#3 Industry structure, business model, financial profile and management

Elekta has a good industry, a second-best position in it, an average financial profile with excellent cash characteristics, and a management team proven on cost and unproven on growth; these foundations support a margin thesis and no more.

The industry structure is attractive for margins and unattractive for Elekta's share. Two companies hold 80 to 90 percent of the market. Regulation, R&D and service networks keep ordinary entrants out, machines are replaced every 10 to 14 years, and the leader prices for margin and competes through bundles and an ecosystem rather than list-price cuts. That structure lets a number two earn a mid-teens margin.

The same structure pulls share mechanically towards the larger, better-integrated player. Doctors train on Varian's interface, and Siemens opens hospital boardrooms through its imaging business; in China, share is pulled towards a state-favoured local maker. Varian's radiotherapy sales are about two and a half times Elekta's, and Varian's share has risen about ten points in recent years, while Elekta's share of new US sales has fallen from above 20 percent to below 15 percent.

The business model and moats are defensive, and defence is enough for this thesis. Service is about 44 percent of sales; contracts cover about 70 percent of roughly 7,500 installed systems; software subscriptions convert at price uplifts of 50 to 80 percent with no attrition so far; and two niches are near-monopolies (Gamma Knife holds about 97 percent of its segment, brachytherapy about 65 percent). These features protect the installed base and the margin. They do not win new accounts in the core linac market, where scale and software are Elekta's weaknesses.

The insight that reconciles the attractive structure with the weak position: the structural bear case, a slow loss of unit share, is already inside the forecast. Half of forecast revenue growth is price, so the base case embeds volume growth of 2 to 2.5 percent a year against market unit growth of 4 to 6 percent. Any surprise on share can therefore only come from Elekta losing less share than assumed. If Elekta merely held its unit share, revenue growth would be about two points a year higher: roughly SEK 360m of sales, SEK 120m to 140m of EBIT and SEK 0.24 to 0.29 of EPS (5 to 6 percent) for each year that the share held.

The evidence that Elekta might hold share is still launch-period evidence. Over 25 percent of US Evo orders are wins from competitors, but nothing shows whether those wins came from Varian or from Accuray's shrinking base, which is the easier and less durable source. The implication: on share, the plausible surprise is upward, and the forecast does not need it.

The financial profile combines average margins, good cash generation and a clean balance sheet. Elekta's margins are mediocre for medical technology (Varian alone earns 18 to 19 percent), and its returns on capital are respectable only after the write-offs (about 14 to 15 percent post-tax on the adjusted base, against 6 percent as reported in FY25). The unusual strength is cash: customers' advance payments of SEK 4.2bn to 4.4bn mean the business runs on negative working capital, and net debt is only about 1.2 times EBITDA on the company's measure.

Customer advances are also a hidden form of operating leverage on orders. A year of orders 15 percent lower could unwind SEK 0.5bn to 0.7bn of advances. Elekta is a cash-return and margin business, not a reinvestment compounder: its record of capital put into new platforms (Unity, cloud software, Kaiku) is the SEK 1.4bn written off.

Management is strong on action and short on record. The chief executive's first twelve months are those of a top-quartile turnaround operator, and his past career fits Elekta's present split exactly: at 3Shape he held margins of 35 to 40 percent through Chinese price dumping and fell short of his owners' growth hopes. Management's goals are sized for repair (the targets are in #4), not conquest. Culture is the weak point (#2).

Governance is mixed. The founder holds 30.2 percent of the votes on 5.7 percent of the capital; that control enabled the reset and also means that no takeover bid can succeed without him. Industry experts speculate about an imaging group buying Elekta, but that speculation is not a floor under the shares.

Against the market. A multiple in the bottom fifth of its ten-year range says the market sees a structurally squeezed number two. I agree on share. I disagree that the share loss impairs the thesis over two years, because the thesis is priced on margin and the forecast already gives up the share.

Strongest counter-case. No precedent in the research shows a number two closing a margin gap to the leader while losing share. Vendor-neutral AI planning tools are commoditising the software lock-in that protects both incumbents. Scale is the defining advantage in this industry: ViewRay failed despite good technology.

What would change my view. Service customers moving to third-party providers, or attrition appearing in software subscriptions, would break the defensive moat. A stabilising US share of new sales would turn a margin case into a growth case.

Score: 47, set by the Rater. A concentrated, high-barrier duopoly with a 44% service annuity, 70% contract coverage and two niche near-monopolies, but Elekta is the sub-scale number two whose unit share is pulled mechanically towards Varian and United Imaging, with a software gap, mediocre margins and a reinvestment record of SEK 1.4bn written off, so the return on new capital is poor; management is proven on cost, not growth, and culture is weak. Reported ROIC of -3.8% (5th percentile) overstates the weakness because of write-offs, but the adjusted 14-15% post-tax is only respectable and margins have been unpredictable; coherent with the four groups at 45-52, it sits just below Xvivo's genuine barriers and above IMCD's leveraged moat.

#4 Guidance, expectations management and the record of delivery

Elekta's margin guidance is conservative and likely to be beaten, its sales guidance is merely realistic, its expectations management has become prudent, and its record of delivery is new on profit and still poor on revenue.

The guidance and targets. FY27 guidance is constant-currency sales growth of 2 to 4 percent and an adjusted EBIT margin of 12.5 to 13.5 percent (FY26: 12.3 percent). The targets for FY29, set in June 2026, are mid-single-digit compound sales growth, an EBIT margin of 14 to 16 percent, free cash flow of about 10 percent of sales and a payout of at least half of net income.

The top of the FY27 margin guidance requires no underlying improvement on last year. After Q1's margin of 11.2 percent, reaching the top of the range needs a margin of about 14.1 percent across Q2 to Q4, against 13.9 percent in the same quarters a year earlier, when the savings were absent from two of those quarters. The expected Q2 tariff refund alone is worth about 20 basis points on those three quarters. Reaching only the bottom of the range would need margins to fall by more than a point year on year.

The FY27 sales guidance is realistic, not conservative. After Q1's organic decline of 2 percent, the bottom of the range needs organic growth of about 3.1 percent in Q2 to Q4. The base case has about 3.2 percent and lands at 2.1 percent for the year, at the edge of the range. Three brokers preview Q2 organic growth of 2.3 to 3.0 percent, against a prior-year quarter that fell 4 percent.

The chief executive's behaviour is that of a manager who lets results run ahead of a wide range. He reiterated guidance, and did not raise it, after a 26 percent EBIT beat in Q1, and he declined to give margin targets before the capital markets day. Philips's new chief executive behaved the same way: Philips guided a margin of 11.3 to 11.8 percent and delivered 12.3 percent.

Elekta's record of delivery splits cleanly into a poor five-year record and a good, short record under the new chief executive. Over five years the record is the worst in its peer set. Under the new chief executive (four quarters) the pattern is unbroken and different: revenue below consensus every time, profit at or above consensus every time. The company has never raised guidance in the period covered by the research files.

Five years: worst record in its peer set

  • Five-year plan: 7%+ growth targeted, about 1% delivered
  • Guidance cut in February 2025
  • 21% EBIT miss; shares -18% in a day

The base rate for the 25 November report is organic sales a little light, profit in line or better, and guidance kept. The margin range is more likely to be exceeded than formally raised. The sales range is at risk of being narrowed to its lower half. The mid-term growth target is above the base case (about 3.5 percent a year at constant currency) and is the likeliest of the company's statements to be softened, though not within a year. The base case meets the mid-term margin target in its lower half (14.4 percent in FY29).

Against the market. Consensus sits near the top of the margin range and treats the top as a ceiling ("little room is left for margin surprises", Jefferies). I think the top of the range is closer to the floor of likely outcomes. On organic sales I agree with consensus, which Jefferies reads at 1.9 percent, below the guided range (see end-note 2).

Strongest counter-case. The margin range already contains about 50 basis points of tariff refunds; materials and wages turn from a help to a hindrance in the second half; and a single slipped installation in April moves the year's margin by more than all of its operating leverage. A company that cut guidance for exactly that reason in February 2025 can cut its sales guidance again.

What would change my view. A Q2 or Q3 gross margin below about 39.5 percent excluding refunds while solutions sales grow, or a cut to sales guidance accompanied by weak Americas orders rather than by installation timing.

Score: 44, set by the Rater. The two-to-three-year record weighs heavily: a guidance cut in February 2025, a 21% EBIT miss, a five-year plan of 7%+ growth that delivered about 1%, and no guidance raise in memory; under the new CEO four quarters show profit at or above consensus every time but revenue below it every time by 2-5%. Current margin guidance is conservative (the top needs no underlying improvement) while sales guidance is merely realistic and may be narrowed down, so, a touch below the Guidance group's 46 and the Sell-side group's 50, it sits below Sdiptech's untested new targets and just above Instalco's documented over-promising.

#5 Does revenue growth lead to outsized profit growth?

Elekta's business model has modest multi-year operating leverage, real but uneven pricing power, a spent cost-out lever and a small financial tailwind; profit outgrows revenue by a factor of one and a half to two, driven by the gross margin, which is also where the case can fail.

The answer is yes in FY27 for a one-off reason, modestly thereafter, and the lever that matters is not the one most people quote.

Operating leverage is real within a year and small across years. With a gross margin near 40 percent and operating costs fixed in the short run, one extra percent of revenue adds about 3 percent to EBIT. Brokers quote that figure, but it does not describe the multi-year path, because operating costs will not stay flat. After years of pay rises near 0.3 percent, with R&D held at about 10 percent of a growing sales line and a US commercial build-out, operating costs should grow about 3.5 percent a year. At revenue growth of 4 to 4.5 percent, the cost ratio then improves by only 20 to 30 basis points a year. The same arithmetic runs in reverse: at revenue growth of 1 percent the EBIT margin would fall by about 60 basis points a year.

Pricing power is the true engine, and it is uneven. Elekta has demonstrated pricing power where it has an installed base (service prices rise about 4 percent a year; software conversions carry large uplifts). It has newly asserted pricing power in hardware, where Evo closes a historical 20 percent price discount to Varian but does not yet command a premium. Pricing power is absent in China and in price-led emerging markets. Net of input inflation, price adds roughly half a point of sales to gross profit each year, and price is the reason the gross margin rises at all in the forecast. Hardware price reaches revenue 12 to 18 months after the quote, so pricing decisions of 2025 and 2026 show in FY28 and FY29.

The cost-out lever is spent. The large overhead cut is done. What remains is a slow cost-of-goods programme (dual sourcing, and renegotiating with single-source suppliers who, in the chief executive's words, "took advantage"), worth perhaps 30 to 40 basis points of gross margin a year before inflation, much of which inflation will absorb. A second large overhead cut would signal that revenue had disappointed.

Financial leverage is a small, steady help. Net interest falls from SEK 356m in FY26 towards SEK 250m by FY29 as debt is repaid, adding about one point a year to EPS growth. Capacity for share buybacks builds up (#6).

Five feedback loops shape the margin over time, and one of them is a trap. Two loops reinforce the margin slowly and dependably: the installed base reprices at each renewal and conversion, and the accounting reset lowers future amortisation. One loop works slowly against Elekta: the pull of share towards Varian. One loop is dormant and valuable: credibility, in which a delivered year raises estimates, higher estimates raise the multiple, a higher multiple raises the value of staff equity, and more valuable equity eases the talent problem. The trap is price discipline that loses volume, under-absorbs fixed cost and tempts management back into discounting.

Reinforcing, slow and dependableAccounting resetlowers future amortisation

Dormant and valuableCredibilitydelivered year → estimates → multiple → staff equity → talent

In the base case, profit grows about one and a half to two times as fast as revenue after FY27, and the excess comes from the gross margin and lower interest more than from volume. In FY27 the cost reset lifts EBIT 15 percent on revenue up 3 percent. From FY28, EBIT grows about 5.5 to 8 percent a year on revenue growth of 4 to 4.5 percent, and EPS grows 8 to 10 percent a year.

Against the market. Brokers' sensitivities imply that a revenue recovery brings a strong margin response. I think the brokers over-state the effect of volume and under-state the effect of price. If revenue recovers through hardware, the mix dilutes the gross margin (service earns perhaps 50 percent and solutions perhaps 33 percent, on our estimates) even as fixed costs are better absorbed.

Strongest counter-case. Q4 FY26 printed an 18.9 percent EBIT margin at peak volume, which shows what full absorption of fixed cost can do; a genuine volume recovery could deliver more operating leverage than I allow.

What would change my view. A gross margin that rises while solutions sales grow faster than service would show that price and mix are stronger than assumed. Price concessions appearing in the gross margin would show that "pricing power breaks before demand does".

Score: 60, set by the Rater. Within a year the structure has real gearing (a gross margin near 40% on short-run fixed operating costs, so 1% of revenue moves EBIT about 3%), pricing power proven on the installed base (service about 4% a year, software conversions at 50-80% uplifts) and now asserted in hardware with Evo, plus a slow installed-base repricing loop and interest falling by about a point of EPS growth a year. It is held near the ordinary mix because operating costs will grow about 3.5% a year, cost-out is spent, a hardware-led recovery dilutes the gross margin, the gearing has run in reverse before (gross margin 45.9% to 37.1%) and EPS grows only about twice revenue after FY27, the median ratio; above the Economic strength group's 45 because the leverage is structural, near the Financial forecasts group's 55.

#6 Forecast financials

The forecasts show a clean break from history in margin, EPS and cash on only a modest improvement in revenue; about two-thirds of three-year earnings growth rests on demonstrated strengths, and the central path sits on consensus.

EPS growth is double-digit from FY26 to FY29 but not from FY27 onwards, and revenue growth is not double-digit at all. EPS grows about 13 percent a year from FY26 to FY29, and just under 10 percent a year (about 9 percent) from FY27 to FY31. Revenue grows 4 percent a year, against 2.3 percent a year over the previous six years.

The forecasts are clearly better than the past on every line except revenue. The EBIT margin moves from a trendless band of 10.3 to 13.9 percent to a rising 13.7 to 15.0 percent. Free cash flow roughly doubles as a share of sales. The gap between reported and adjusted EPS, SEK 4.81 in FY26, shrinks to a few tenths of a krona. On a market value of about SEK 23.8bn, the free cash flow yield is 6.4 percent in FY27, rising to 7.4 percent in FY29, and the dividend yield is 4.0 percent.

About two-thirds of the EPS growth from FY26 to FY29 rests on strengths already demonstrated; the other third rests on judgements J2 and J3. Roughly a quarter of the growth comes from near-certain items below EBIT (lower interest and a normal tax rate). Roughly 45 percent comes from margin (mostly the banked FY27 step, then the gross margin). Roughly 30 percent comes from revenue, half of which is installed-base pricing.

My range of plausible EPS outcomes (the "cone") is narrow and symmetric for FY27, and wider and tilted down for FY28. For FY27 the cone is SEK 3.90 to 4.45 around the base case of SEK 4.18, roughly symmetric. For FY28 the cone is SEK 3.85 to 5.00 around SEK 4.51, tilted down. The FY28 tilt arises because the identifiable negatives are specific, dated and correlated (a pricing response, weaker volume and under-absorbed cost would arrive together), while the positives are broader and independent of one another.

The sum of FY27 and FY28 EPS is more predictable than either year alone. Fourth-quarter timing shifts about SEK 0.15 of EPS between the two years for each 1 percent of annual revenue that slips across the 30 April year-end.

Against the company's own FY29 targets, the base case misses on growth, meets the margin target in its lower half and falls a little short on free cash flow (9.4 against about 10 percent of sales in FY29). The growth target is not part of this case.

Two parts of the forecast should be held loosely.

  • Buybacks. The model starts buybacks in FY30 (SEK 500m, then SEK 600m). They are authorised but not mooted, and they supply about 4 percent of FY31 EPS. The buyback option also cuts the other way: net debt falls to roughly half of EBITDA by FY29, and free cash flow exceeds the dividend by SEK 0.6bn to 0.8bn a year, about 3 percent of the market value, so an earlier start is possible and would be new information.
  • Capitalised development. The model treats the accounting drag from lower capitalisation as ending after FY27. One broker models amortisation above capitalisation in FY28, a further 20 to 50 basis points of margin drag, which is part of why the FY28 cone is tilted down.

Against the market. On the central figures there is almost no difference from consensus: revenue about 1 percent below, FY27 EBIT about 3 percent above and EPS 1 to 2 percent above. The disagreement is one line (the margin) in one year (FY27). I agree with consensus on FY28 and FY29 and say so plainly: the base case reaches consensus earnings with slightly more margin and slightly less revenue.

Strongest counter-case. Upward: DNB Carnegie's FY29 EPS of SEK 5.60 shows what the company's targets deliver if growth arrives. Downward: Goldman Sachs and UBS, near SEK 4.16 to 4.18 for FY29, show a margin that stalls near 12 to 13 percent.

What would change my view. The triggers are those of judgements J1 to J4 in #9.

Score: 77, set by the Rater. About 12% sits in the 10-15% B band, and it is honest on the underlying base, all organic, with the margin moving above anything in the annual record (13.7% to 15.0% against a 10.3-13.9% band) and free cash flow nearly doubling as a share of sales. It is placed low in the band because the growth is front-loaded (FY27 +21% from the banked cost reset, then 8-10% a year, about 9% from FY27 to FY31) on revenue of only about 4% a year, half of it price.

#7 Scope for upgrades to guidance, estimates and the narrative over 6 to 12 months

There is scope for small, broad, late upgrades to FY27 estimates and for the bear narrative to lose its footing, concentrated in the next six months; beyond that window the scope narrows and the tilt turns slightly negative.

A beat of the margin guidance is more likely than a formal raise (#4), and early March 2027 is the earliest realistic date for a raise. A first raise would matter out of proportion to its size, because the company has none on record.

Estimate upgrades should be small, positive in breadth and late.

  • Size. The gap between the base case and consensus is the FY27 margin, worth about 3 percent of EBIT and 2 percent of EPS in FY27, and 1 to 2 percent of EPS in FY28 and FY29.
  • Breadth. Of the eight FY27 EPS estimates that FactSet shows, five are below the base case, one is level and two are above; for FY28, six of ten are below. Three estimates pre-date the turn in exchange rates, and two of those three are among the lowest, so refreshing them lifts breadth mechanically.
  • Timing. Brokers anchor on the top of guidance, so upgrades should arrive when the fourth quarter is in sight, with the March or May reports. I put the probability that FY27 EPS is raised by 2 percent or more across the next two reports at about 45 percent, held at 40 percent and cut at 15 percent.
  • After May 2027 the tilt reverses. FY28 guidance will be a first-time guide, set after the tariff refunds end, with hedge rates lower and Accela on the market, so management will naturally build in a buffer. I put the probability that FY28 EPS is cut by 2 percent or more between May 2027 and March 2028 at about 35 percent, against 25 percent that it is raised.

Currency will blur the signal from estimate revisions. Revisions for Elekta have been driven by exchange rates as much as by operations: one broker cut EPS by 11 to 16 percent on currency in May 2025, and another raised EPS by 2 to 4 percent this month. A 3 to 5 percent move in the krona changes consensus EPS by as much as our whole operating difference with consensus. Investors should therefore judge delivery on organic growth, the gross margin excluding refunds and the cash margin, not on the direction of revisions to reported sales.

The available change in narrative is on the bear side, because "margin delivered, sales unproven" is already the sell-side's story. Four of eleven ratings are Sells, with targets of SEK 41 to 52, and the bear case rests on a margin stuck near 12 percent. A delivered FY27 margin at or above 13.5 percent removes that bear case arithmetically. At Philips, underweight ratings went from a third of the total to none on delivered guidance. My evidence on the bear case is indirect: the research files hold no notes from the three named brokers with Sell ratings and no direct investor commentary, so I read the bear case through the cautious Hold-rated brokers and industry experts.

The mismatch that defines the next six months: the thesis is a margin thesis, but margin beats alone no longer move the shares. The 26 percent EBIT beat in Q1 moved the shares 1 percent on the day because sales missed, while profit misses, guidance cuts and order shortfalls have produced the large falls. Margin delivery alone may therefore go unrewarded, particularly after a 19 percent share price rise since late September. The precedents show what does get rewarded: a sequence of beats and raises. Demant's multiple rose from about 15 to over 19 times within about eight months of its first upgraded guidance; Philips took about a year from its restructuring plan.

Against the market. The cautious half of the sell-side expects no margin surprise; I expect a modest one. On FY28 and beyond I am no more optimistic than the market, and I think the market reflects the dated FY28 negatives less well than the FY27 positives.

Strongest counter-case. The upgrades could net to nothing: FY27 upgrades of 2 percent offset by a cautious FY28 guide, with currency deciding the sign. That outcome is plausible and would leave the shares dependent on the cohort's multiple.

What would change my view. A guidance raise on 25 November, which I would read as a change in management's posture; or, negatively, a first profit miss under this chief executive.

Score: 55, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, is more likely beaten than raised (a raise about 15% likely in November and 40% by March, an outcome above the 13.5% margin top about 55%) while the sales range may be narrowed down; consensus FY27 EPS is about 2% below the base case (45% raised, 15% cut), a raise of about half the revenue growth rate, and the bear narrative can lose its premise. Inside the window the first FY28 guide in late May 2027 leans cautious (FY28 cut 35% against raised 25%), so, matching the fourth set's 55, the scope sits below Hexatronic's and just above Spie's.

#8 Current momentum: guidance, estimates, narrative, price, and peers

Momentum is strong in the share price and the narrative, flat in estimates and guidance, and weak in peers' earnings; the recent strength is largely the cohort's, so it is not yet evidence of Elekta's own progress.

Guidance momentum: none yet. Management reiterated guidance after Q1 and did not raise it.

Sell-side earnings momentum is flat, and the dashboard's pinned grade is D (snapshot of 14 November 2026). Consensus EPS for FY28 is unchanged over one month, up 3 percent over three months and down 2 percent over six months. Sales estimates are down 6 percent over twelve months and have just turned up because of currency. The share of Buy ratings is 38 percent and has fallen six points, and the mean target price (SEK 58.38) is below the share price.

Price momentum is strong on the raw readings, although the dashboard's pinned grade is also D (same snapshot). The shares are up 47 percent in twelve months and 17 percent in three, within 2 percent of the 52-week high, and 17 percent above a 200-day moving average that has risen in ten of the last twelve months; relative strength is at the 80th percentile of the universe. The pinned grade and the raw readings disagree; I report both and use the pinned grade as given.

Narrative momentum has improved, and the improvement is already paid for. In three months the story has moved from "value trap at an all-time-low multiple" to "self-help margin recovery". The capital markets day in June was received with scepticism (the shares fell 7 percent the next day); the Q1 margin and the cohort's rally changed the tone.

Peers' share prices are up, but peers' estimates are not. The sector's median share price rose about 20 percent in the three months to late October as money rotated into European medical-technology capital goods. Siemens Healthineers, however, carries a pinned earnings-momentum grade of F: it guides flat adjusted EPS, and its radiotherapy division's margin fell from 17.1 to 13.8 percent in the September quarter on inflation, currency and mix. Philips carries D on both technical and earnings momentum.

Over the last three months Elekta's share price momentum has been borrowed from the cohort, and borrowed momentum can be reclaimed. Momentum is strong in the price and absent in the estimates, for Elekta and for its cohort alike. Over twelve months Elekta's outperformance was its own, because the cohort was flat; over the last three months it came from the cohort. The cohort re-rated on sector rotation and can de-rate on rotation, and Siemens AG's planned distribution of its Siemens Healthineers stake is a share-supply event for the group.

What would change my view. Upward revisions of 3 percent or more to FY28 EPS with the share of Buy ratings rising would be real momentum. The shares falling back below the 200-day moving average on an in-line report would show that the move was rotation.

One measure in the bottom fifth and one in the top fifth is mixed, so C: the price is strong (up 47% in twelve months, near its high, 17% above a rising 200-day average) and the narrative has improved, but guidance is only reiterated, FY28 EPS is flat over one month, +3% over three and -2% over six, the buy share has fallen to 38% and the mean target is below the price. Placed in the lower half because the last three months' strength was borrowed from the cohort while peers' earnings momentum is weak (Siemens Healthineers F, Philips D).

#9 Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and expectations

The case is simple and well covered for FY27 and of middling risk thereafter, with the risk concentrated in the gross margin, the fourth quarter and a share price prone to gaps; the risks are trackable on the margin side and largely opaque on competition.

The forecasts are highly simple for FY27 and moderately simple afterwards. FY27 has one driver, the cost saving, and that driver is banked. FY28 and FY29 depend on one line and one condition. The line is the gross margin, which is itself the net of six forces: price, cost-of-goods savings, input inflation, mix, refunds and currency. The condition is organic growth near 4 percent, concentrated in one product and two regions, each contested by a named competitor.

The five judgements, step by step.

J1. The FY27 margin lands above the top of guidance. Q2 to Q4 revenue is about SEK 13,680m, and the base case implies a Q2 to Q4 gross margin of about 39.5 percent including the Q2 refund, some 160 basis points below Q1's underlying level.

  • If the gross margin is 0.5 point lower: 13,680 x 0.5% = SEK 68m less EBIT, so FY27 EBIT is about SEK 2,295m (a 13.3 percent margin). After 23 percent tax and over 382.1m shares, EPS falls SEK 0.14 to about SEK 4.04, which is consensus.
  • If a gross margin of about 40.3 percent is held (0.8 point higher, and still below Q1's 41.1 percent): EBIT rises SEK 109m to about SEK 2,470m (a 14.3 percent margin), and EPS rises SEK 0.22 to about SEK 4.40.

J2. The gross margin holds near 40.5 percent in FY28. One point of gross margin on FY28 revenue of SEK 17,907m is SEK 179m.

  • EBIT falls from SEK 2,494m to SEK 2,315m (the margin from 13.9 to 12.9 percent; EBIT -7 percent).
  • Pre-tax profit falls by the same SEK 179m; at 22.5 percent tax, net income falls SEK 139m, and EPS falls SEK 0.36 to SEK 4.15 (-8 percent). Free cash flow falls by about the same SEK 139m (-8.5 percent).
  • At today's multiple, the EPS loss is worth about SEK 5 a share.

J3. Organic growth reaches 4 percent in FY28. Two points less growth is SEK 358m of revenue.

  • At a 40 percent gross margin with costs fixed, EBIT falls SEK 143m (-6 percent; a 13.4 percent margin), and EPS falls SEK 0.29 to SEK 4.22 (-6 percent). If the shortfall is all hardware (about a 33 percent gross margin), EPS falls SEK 0.24.
  • If growth stayed near 1 percent while costs inflate, the EBIT margin would be about a point lower and EPS about 10 percent lower, and the shortfall would compound into FY29.

J4. The dollar and US tariffs stay roughly where they are. A 1 percent move in the dollar is worth about SEK 18m (per the annual report) to SEK 30m (per broker estimates) of operating profit, and FY28 was only thinly hedged at the last disclosure.

  • A dollar 5 percent weaker against the krona and sterling costs SEK 90m to 150m of EBIT (4 to 6 percent), or SEK 0.18 to 0.30 of EPS.
  • A Section 232 duty of 10 to 25 percent on perhaps SEK 750m of transfer value costs SEK 75m to 190m a year (45 to 110 basis points of gross margin), or SEK 0.15 to 0.39 of EPS until contract tariff clauses and repricing recover the cost over several months.

J5. The market pays a cohort multiple. At the January 2028 column of the model, two-year-forward EPS is about SEK 5.27, so each 1.0 times of multiple is worth SEK 5.3 a share, 8 percent of today's price. The spread between a trough multiple of 11 times and a broadening multiple of 16 times is SEK 26 a share, 42 percent of today's price, which is larger than the effect of any single fundamental judgement above (see #11).

J5, the multiple: each 1.0x is SEK 5.3 a share, 8% of today's price.
11x to 16x: a spread of SEK 26, 42% of today's price, larger than any single fundamental judgement.

Six fragilities sit under the forecasts.

  • The line on which the case rests is the line that failed before. Elekta's gross margin fell from 45.9 to 37.1 percent in the year to Q1 FY22. The mechanism is asymmetric: costs arrive at once, while hardware price increases follow 9 to 12 months later and reach revenue a year after that.
  • The fourth quarter is concentrated. Q4 carries about 28 percent of sales and 40 percent of EBIT, and it is reported after the six-month monitoring window.
  • The risks are correlated. A US pricing response, weaker volume and under-absorbed fixed cost would arrive together, and so would the talent and credibility loops (#5).
  • Cash depends on orders through customer advances (#3). No one on the sell-side discusses the dependence.
  • The reset depends on people. Two key individuals lead a strained organisation.
  • "One-off" charges recur. A further impairment (of Unity, a software asset or an emerging-market receivable) is perhaps a one-in-four event over 18 months; it would cost credibility, not cash.

The case is easy to track on the margin and hard to track on competition. The company now quantifies tariff refunds, currency effects, the capitalisation effect and a cash margin each quarter, and it publishes forward hedge rates, so a deviation in cost or gross margin can be seen and traced within a quarter. Nothing observable sits between a Varian launch or a Siemens bundle and Elekta's US revenue, except Elekta's own regional orders, which lead revenue by two to four quarters; price concessions are invisible until they appear in the gross margin. Five thresholds keep the case on track.

The share price is prone to sudden gaps. The stock has moved 15 percent or more in a single session on results several times, in both directions. Short interest was historically near a fifth of the free float; the current level is not in the research files. A fall to a trough multiple of 10.5 to 11 times on today's forward earnings would take the shares to SEK 49 to 51 (about -20 percent), and a 10 percent earnings cut on top would take them to SEK 44 to 46.

The sector's accidents are gross-margin, policy and scale accidents, not demand cycles. Radiotherapy demand is not very cyclical. The sector's accidents have been gross-margin accidents (inflation in FY22; Siemens' radiotherapy margin this autumn), policy accidents (China's freeze; tariffs) and failures of sub-scale players (Accuray, ViewRay). Slow growers that miss are punished twice, in the multiple and in the earnings; Elekta's 72 percent fall from its 2021 high is the example.

The can-do reading: most of these risks are slow, visible and sized, and time works for the holder. The balance sheet is sound, 44 percent of sales is service, and the year in progress is covered by the banked saving. The fast risks (a results-day gap; a tariff decision) are share-price risks more than value risks. Each year adds about 14 percent of earnings-plus-dividend return while the margin holds.

Against the market. The market watches revenue and Accela. I think the larger and less-watched risk is the FY28 gross margin, and that the near-term competitive risk is smaller than the share price reaction to any sales miss would imply.

Strongest counter-case. The case may be riskier than it looks, because the base case is the point where everything nets to zero, and in Elekta's history things have not netted to zero.

What would change my view. Two quarters of gross margin above 40 percent excluding refunds with growth in solutions sales would retire the central fragility and move the case towards low risk.

Score: 50, set by the Rater. The FY27 EPS cone is narrow (SEK 3.90-4.45, about +/-7%) and rests on one banked driver, with low leverage (1.2x) and little cyclicality; but FY28's cone widens to about -15%/+11% and tilts down, resting on a gross margin that has collapsed before, organic growth contested by named competitors, correlated dated negatives, 40% of EBIT in the fourth quarter, opaque competitive transmission, two key people and a share price that gaps 15% on results with about 20% to a trough multiple. Between the first-layer Risks group's 40 and the later layers' 50, it sits below NKT's visible backlog and just above IMCD's leveraged downgrade record.

#10 Where the stock is in its lifecycle

The stock is turning up and has completed the multiple's recovery from the trough; it has not yet broadened, and the events that would take it there fall between March and late May 2027.

My placement: late in the Turning-up phase, at the door of Broadening.

The path so far.

  • Bottoming (April to October 2025). The multiple touched 9.9 times, estimates for FY27 to FY29 were cut 27 to 30 percent from their highs, and a new chief executive arrived.
  • Turning up (November 2025 to now). Orders were cleaned, the balance sheet was kitchen-sinked in Q4 FY26, two EBIT beats were reported, the cuts to estimates stopped, and the share price rose from the mid-40s to SEK 62.40. The last leg of the rise, since late September, was the multiple catching up with the cohort's.

The thesis has not yet broadened, because none of the three conditions for broadening has been met. A thesis broadens when estimates rise, the sceptics convert and the evidence extends from the first proof (margin) to the second (revenue). Instead, estimates are flat, the share of Buy ratings is falling, the company has not raised guidance, and revenue has yet to show organic growth this year. The dashboard's rule places the stock in Broadening; I place it one step earlier, because the rule reads the share price and I am reading the estimates.

Four dated events could move the stock forward into Broadening.

  • 25 November 2026: the Q2 report, with a return to organic growth likely and guidance kept.
  • Early February 2027: Siemens Healthineers' report, showing Varian's growth and the timing of Accela's approval.
  • Early March 2027: the Q3 report, with nine months in hand and a first guidance raise possible.
  • Late May 2027: the fourth quarter, the first delivered guidance year in several, and FY28 guidance.

I put the chance that the stock is clearly in Broadening by mid-2027 at about one in three: Broadening needs a first raise or a beat of the range and a constructive FY28 guide.

Stalling, not collapsing, is the live alternative, at about one in four. Stalling would look like organic growth stuck at 1 to 2 percent, a gross margin slipping below 39.5 percent, a cautious FY28 guide and a multiple drifting back to 11 to 12 times as the cohort's rotation fades. Collapsing would need the margin leg itself to break, which the FY27 arithmetic makes unlikely within a year.

The lifecycle implication for valuation: a stock that is turning up, with forecasts still uncertain in the year that matters, belongs in the lower half of its multiple range. That placement is the bridge to the fair multiple in #11.

Against the market and the dashboard. The share price says Broadening; the sell-side's ratings say the turn is not yet believed. I think both are partly right: the turn is real, and it has not yet earned the next phase.

Strongest counter-case. Broadening may have begun in August with the Q1 report, and the share price may simply be reporting it ahead of the analysts, as share prices in this sector tend to.

What would change my view. Upgrades to FY28 estimates with a rising share of Buy ratings would move the stock forward to Broadening; a profit miss, or a cut to sales guidance with weak US orders, would move it back to Stalling.

Score: 62, set by the Rater. The memo's late Turning Up is right against both the computed Bottoming and the dashboard's Broadening: the margin turn is real and two EBIT beats are banked, but estimates are flat, the buy share is falling, no raise has come and the multiple has already recovered from 9.9x to 13.4x, so part of the good news is priced. Broadening by mid-2027 is about one in three against Stalling at one in four, so it sits below Kerry's steady Reinforcing and just above Nexans' paused momentum.

#11 The fair multiple

Viewforth's guideline multiple of 24.09 times is not a multiple I can support; about 14 times is fair for a stock that is turning up, about 16 times if the thesis broadens, and 10.5 to 11 times if it stalls.

The guideline. Viewforth's guideline fair multiple for the dashboard's phase (Broadening) is 24.09 times two-year-forward earnings, the 80th percentile of the stock's own ten-year history. At SEK 62.40 the model's multiple is 13.4 times (13.65 times on FactSet consensus), so the guideline is 80 percent above today's multiple (see end-note 3).

The guideline is too high for this stock in this phase, by a wide margin, for four reasons.

  1. The ten-year history describes two different companies. Before 2022 the shares traded at a median of about 22 times for a growth story (the Unity MR-linac, a linac combined with magnetic resonance imaging, and organic growth of 7 to 9 percent) that ended in guidance cuts and write-offs. Since January 2022 the median multiple is 13.0 times. All eleven months at or above 24.09 times fall between June 2018 and July 2021; the multiple has not been above 17.6 times since August 2022, nor above 16.0 times since January 2024. An 80th percentile drawn across both regimes is therefore a statistic of the first regime.
  2. The peers do not support the guideline. The better-placed leader, Siemens Healthineers, trades at 13.9 times, at the very bottom of its own ten-year range, and Philips trades at 14.8 times. A multiple of 24 times would put the number two at a 70 percent premium to the number one. In 2019 Elekta traded at a 30 percent premium to Varian, and that premium did not hold.
  3. Elekta's fundamentals are not those of a 24-times stock. A 24-times multiple pays for double-digit growth with rising estimates and a long reinvestment runway. The base case is EPS growth of about 9 percent on revenue growth of 4 percent, estimates on consensus, and a business that returns cash because its reinvestment record is poor. Every earlier period in which Elekta traded above 20 times was unsupported by what followed.
  4. The lifecycle phase is one step earlier than the guideline rule assumes (#10). By the framework's own logic, a turning-up stock sits lower in its range.

The dashboard's own readings point the same way. Its valuation bands label 22.8 times "defendable" and 27.9 times "mania", so 24.09 times lies beyond the defendable band. Its pinned valuation grade is A (snapshot of 14 November 2026), because the multiple is at the 20th percentile of its ten-year history; but Master Rating 8, total shareholder return relative to valuation, is F on the last memo's return re-based to today's price. The valuation grade reads the old regime; the return rating reads what the forecasts can deliver.

What I think is fair, by state of the case.

State of the case Fair two-year-forward multiple Reasoning
Stalling 10.5 to 11x Just below the five-year 10th percentile (11.4x); the level of mid-2025
Turning up (today) about 14x (13 to 15x) The five-year median (13.6x); the cohort's band; a 4 to 5 percent grower with a mid-teens margin, 4 percent yield and cash-backed earnings
Broadening, delivered about 16x The 80th percentile of the last five years, i.e. the guideline's own rule applied to the regime the company is in; the ten-year "conservative" band
Reinforcing (growth of 5 percent or more sustained two years) about 18x The ten-year median; needs the revenue leg and software progress

A constructive suggestion on the guideline rule: apply the same 80th-percentile rule to the last five years instead of ten, which gives about 16 times. I can defend 16 times as the multiple for a broadening that has actually been delivered.

Against the market. The market pays 13.4 to 13.8 times. Broker targets imply about 9 times (UBS) to 15 times (DNB Carnegie), with the mean near 12.5 times. At 14 times I am slightly above the market's centre, because I think the bear case's margin assumption is about to be disproved, and far below the guideline.

Strongest counter-case for a higher multiple. Turnarounds re-rate quickly once a beat-and-raise sequence starts (Demant; Philips); Elekta's own ten-year median is 18 times; and DNB Carnegie argues that the shares could double if the FY29 targets are met. If earnings grow 10 percent a year, fully backed by cash, with a 4 percent yield and buybacks to come, 16 to 18 times is not unreasonable. I accept that range for the delivered-broadening state. It does not reach 24 times.

What would change my view. Evidence that Elekta is gaining US share through a Varian product cycle, with software attached, would make Elekta a different company and reopen the upper half of the old multiple range. Nothing in the research files points there yet.

Score: 75, set by the Rater. Cheap on the own-range measure and neutral against peers gives B. Placed at the floor of the band because most of the cheapness is deserved: the ten-year range was built in a growth regime that ended in write-offs, the post-2022 median is 13.0x so today's 13.4x is at its regime median, a turning-up stock belongs low in its range, and the memo's fair 14x is only about 4% above the price.

#12 Total shareholder return

Three-quarters of the model's +107 percent return comes from a guideline multiple I do not think the stock will reach; the supportable return is about 17 to 22 percent to January 2028 and about 14 to 15 percent a year over three years, driven by roughly 10 percent earnings growth and a 4 percent dividend yield.

The model's return at the guideline multiple.

Horizon (the model's columns) Total return Annualised From dividends From the multiple From earnings
To 31 January 2028 (the "18-month" column; about 14.5 months away) +107.4% +82.9% +4.0% +80.0% +13.0%
To 31 July 2029 (the "three-year" column; about 2.7 years away) +144.6% +39.2% +13.0% +80.0% +28.6%

The multiple and earnings parts multiply; the dividend part adds.

What drives each part of the return.

  • Earnings (+13 percent to January 2028, then +28.6 percent to July 2029). Two-year-forward EPS rises from about SEK 4.66 today to about SEK 5.27 at the first column and about SEK 6.00 at the second, roughly 10 percent a year. The drivers are those of #6: the banked FY27 step rolling through, a slow margin gain and falling interest. About 4 points of the three-year earnings gain come from buybacks that are not yet mooted.
  • Dividends (+4 percent, then +13 percent). One dividend of SEK 2.50 falls within the first column, and three (SEK 2.50, 2.70 and 2.90) within the second. The dividends are well covered: free cash flow is about 1.6 times the dividend.
  • The multiple (+80 percent at both columns). The multiple part is the guideline's 24.09 times against 13.4 times today, reached at the first column and held. It supplies 80 of the 107 points of the 14-month return and more than half of the three-year return, and for the reasons in #11 it is the part I cannot support.

The same return at other multiples (the model's earnings and dividends, unchanged).

Multiple at the horizon Price, January 2028 Total return to January 2028 Price, July 2029 Total return to July 2029 Annualised
11x (stalling) SEK 58 -3% SEK 66 +19% +6.6%
13.4x (unchanged) SEK 71 +17% SEK 80 +42% +13.8%
14x (my fair multiple today) SEK 74 +22% SEK 84 +48% +15.5%
16x (broadening delivered) SEK 84 +39% SEK 96 +67% +20.9%
24.09x (guideline) SEK 127 +107% SEK 145 +145% +39.2%

How I read the return.

  • The return this work supports is in the middle rows. At an unchanged or fair multiple the shares offer about 17 to 22 percent to January 2028 and about 14 to 15 percent a year to mid-2029. That return is good for a business with these cash characteristics, and it needs only the earnings to be delivered.
  • Over six months the multiple dominates the return. Forward earnings roll up only about 5 percent in half a year, and no dividend is paid before September 2027, so the six-month outcome is mostly the market's reaction to two reports: each turn of multiple, up or down, is worth about 8 percent.
  • A rough probability weighting gives about +20 percent to January 2028. Stalling with a 10 percent earnings shortfall (about one in five to one in four) returns about -12 percent. The base case (about one half) returns +22 percent. Broadening with modest upgrades (about one in five to one in four) returns about +43 percent. The guideline outcome has a probability of a few percent at most. The distribution leans positive over 14 months, because earnings and dividends accrue under every branch, but it is not strongly skewed.
  • The earnings leg has its own range of outcomes (judgements J1 to J4): one point of gross margin is worth about 8 percent of earnings.

Against the market. The mean broker target (SEK 58.38) implies a small negative return, while the model at the guideline multiple implies a doubling. I sit between the two, closer to the brokers' Buy cases (targets of SEK 68 to 70) on a 14-month view, and for a reason those brokers also give: earnings delivery at a modest multiple.

Strongest counter-case. The middle rows may be too high, because they hold the multiple steady while FY28's dated negatives arrive (the stalling row). Or they may be too low, because a first guidance raise could start the credibility loop sooner than I allow (the broadening row).

What would change my view. The dated events listed in #10, which map directly onto the rows of the second table.

Score: 76, set by the Rater. About +20% sits at the floor of the B band and maps to about 75; it is almost all earnings growth of about 10% a year and a 4% dividend yield at an unchanged or fair multiple, rejecting the guideline's +107%, and the three-year check is supportive. Nudged up a point because the weighting runs to about 14.5 months rather than 18, held there by a lower tail of about -12% in the stalling branch with correlated FY28 negatives.

#13 Summary conclusion

Elekta today is a well-evidenced margin recovery inside a second-best competitive position. Management has delivered the part of the case it controls with unusual speed, and the result is visible in the accounts. That delivered recovery carries FY27 by itself and makes the margin guidance conservative. It creates a real, small and near-dated skew towards results above guidance and consensus, and towards the bear case losing its premise, between now and late May 2027.

Beyond late May 2027 the case rests on one strength the company has shown for only two quarters: holding price as hardware volume returns. Against that strength stand a cluster of dated FY28 headwinds and two capable competitors. The FY28 forecasts are consensus, the FY28 range of outcomes tilts down, and the gross margin is the line to watch.

The shares have already been paid for the worry clearing; what remains on offer is about 10 percent earnings growth and a 4 percent yield at a fair multiple. That combination is worth roughly 14 to 15 percent a year, with an option on a broadening of the thesis worth a further two turns of multiple and about 10 percent on FY28 earnings if revenue confirms. The guideline's 24 times is not part of that return.

The decisive information arrives in three steps.
Early March 2027Can the margin range be raised?
Late May 2027Did the year deliver, and how is FY28 guided?
First half of FY28Does the gross margin hold with hardware growing?

The four memo ratings

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 65, set by the Rater. Strong, banked internal forces (topic 2 at 70) surely reach profits, giving a 21% EPS step in FY27, but the external balance is a mild headwind (topic 1 at 46) and the forecast outputs only reach about 12% a year front-loaded and about 9% thereafter on 4% revenue (topic 6 at 77), so clear positive inputs that lift profits just above the Universe's median growth place it in the mid 60s.

Foundations' Robustness: 55, set by the Rater. The industry itself is robust (a high-barrier duopoly, 10-14 year replacement cycles, non-cyclical healthcare demand) and the business has a 44% service annuity, niche near-monopolies, negative working capital and a clean balance sheet, which lifts it above Quality of the business at 47; but a sub-scale number two losing share, a software gap, unstable gross margins, poor reinvestment and a delivery record that is poor over five years and only one year good (topic 4 at 44) keep it below Judges Scientific's 60.

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 68, set by the Rater. The case fits Major CfC Clearing in a middling-quality non-cyclical business on a bottom-quintile multiple in substance (the margin, order-quality and accounting concerns are clearing in the accounts), which Richard places at 65-75 for a mediocre-quality business; it sits in the lower part of that range because today's problems blur the fit (organic sales falling in Q1, continued share loss, a strained organisation), while the already-recovered multiple is a price matter and does not count here.

Case Riskiness: 47, set by the Rater. Over Riskiness and simplicity at 50: FY27 is simple and covered and leverage is low, but these are not paper cuts, since the case after FY27 rests on a gross margin that has failed before, with correlated FY28 negatives, a fourth-quarter concentration and a share price that gaps on results and punishes a slow grower twice, so the equity outcome is a little less predictable than the operating lines.

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
